notes.meaning: A man named Ananias and his wife Sapphira sold a piece of land to give money to the church. Unlike Barnabas, who gave sincerely, this couple acted out of a desire for human praise and attention. They wanted others to view them as deeply spiritual and generous.

differ.view: John Wesley taught that Ananias was not a true believer at all, because genuine believers in the early church were completely united in heart and mind.
Some Reformed teachers hold that Ananias and Sapphira were genuine believers whose earthly lives were cut short as a severe chastisement, while their souls remained saved.

notes.meaning: Ananias secretly kept back some of the sale money for himself, and his wife agreed to the plan. He brought only a part of the sum and laid it before the apostles as if it were the whole amount. The wrongdoing was not in keeping some money, but in pretending to give everything.

Peter received spiritual insight from God and confronted Ananias directly about his dishonesty. He asked why Ananias had allowed Satan to fill his heart so that he lied to the Holy Spirit. Ananias had the power to resist the devil's temptation, yet he chose to carry out the deceit.

Peter reminded Ananias that the land belonged to him before it was sold, and the money remained his own to use as he wished. There was never any rule forcing believers to give up their property. By pretending to give it all, Ananias was not merely deceiving human leaders, but lying directly to God the Holy Spirit.

differ.view: Wesley saw the early church community as having fully given up private goods, viewing Ananias's action as the first sinful attempt to reintroduce private ownership.
Most evangelicals teach that giving up property was entirely voluntary, meaning believers were free to keep their possessions without guilt.

notes.meaning: As soon as Ananias heard Peter's words expose his sin, he fell down and died instantly. Peter did not pronounce a death sentence, but God struck Ananias down in judgment. A deep, reverent fear swept over everyone who heard about what had happened.

The younger men present in the gathering stood up right away to attend to the body. They wrapped Ananias in burial cloths according to Jewish custom and carried him outside the city. He was buried promptly on that very day.

About three hours later, Sapphira arrived where the apostles were gathered. She had no idea that her husband had died and had already been buried. This delay gave her an opportunity to speak the truth, though she remained unaware of the danger.

Peter asked Sapphira directly whether the amount of money brought was the full price received for the land. This question offered her a clear chance to repent and tell the truth. Instead, she stuck to the deceitful plan and confirmed that it was indeed the full price.

Peter asked Sapphira how she and her husband could agree together to test the Spirit of the Lord. Testing God meant acting as if the Holy Spirit could not see through their secret deception. Peter then revealed that the young men who buried her husband were at the door and would carry her out as well.

Sapphira collapsed at Peter's feet and died instantly, just as her husband had. When the young men returned, they found her dead on the floor. They carried her body outside and buried her right beside Ananias.

A profound and holy fear came upon the entire church, which is the gathering of believers, and upon all outsiders who heard the news. God's judgment purified the community and reminded everyone that hypocrisy cannot hide before Him. It taught all believers to take their walk with God seriously.

God worked many miraculous signs and wonders among the people through the hands of the apostles. Meanwhile, the believers gathered regularly with one heart in Solomon's Colonnade, a covered porch in the temple courts. Their deep unity was another clear sign of the Holy Spirit at work.

People outside the church viewed the apostles with great respect and spoke highly of them. Yet outsiders did not dare join the fellowship casually or hypocritically after seeing the judgment on Ananias and Sapphira. The seriousness of the Christian faith kept insincere pretenders away.

Even though insincere people kept their distance, large crowds of sincere men and women put their trust in Jesus. These new converts were added to the Lord and welcomed into the church family. The judgment on sin did not stop the church from growing, but actually drew true believers in.

Because of the amazing miracles taking place, people carried the sick out into the streets on beds and mats. They placed them along the walkways hoping that at least Peter's shadow would touch some of them as he walked past. They believed God's power was present with the apostles in an extraordinary way.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars point out that ancient Mediterranean cultures believed shadows possessed healing or harmful powers, which helps explain why crowds placed the sick where Peter's shadow would fall.

notes.meaning: Crowds began traveling to Jerusalem from neighboring towns and villages, bringing their sick family members and those troubled by evil spirits. The apostles ministered to everyone who came to them. Every single person who was brought received complete healing.

The high priest and his fellow leaders from the party of the Sadducees grew intensely jealous of the apostles' growing influence. The Sadducees rejected the idea that people rise from the dead, so the apostles' message about Jesus rising from death greatly troubled them. Their anger drove them to take forceful action against the disciples.

The temple authorities seized all the apostles and locked them inside the public city jail. They treated these servants of God like common criminals to shame them and keep them quiet. The rulers hoped this imprisonment would put an end to their public ministry.

During the night, an angel sent by the Lord miraculously unlocked the prison doors. The angel led the apostles safely outside past the guards. This rescue showed that God's power easily overcomes human locks, bars, and hostile rulers.

The angel instructed the apostles not to flee into hiding, but to return to the public temple courts. He commanded them to stand openly and preach the full message of this new, eternal life found in Christ. God freed them so they could continue fulfilling their mission with boldness.

At daybreak, the apostles obeyed God's command, entered the temple courtyards, and began teaching the people. Meanwhile, the high priest called together the Sanhedrin, which was the ruling council of Jewish elders, and sent officers to the prison to fetch the prisoners. The rulers planned a trial, unaware that God had already set His servants free.
